issues.description: Constructor signature mismatch and internal inconsistency in the Lights Out (Exercise 4) template: the template class GroverLightsOutPuzzle defines __init__(self, initial_state: list[int]) (requiring an argument), but the class run() docstring and the way run() instantiates/uses the class in the template assume no constructor argument. The solution implementation uses __init__(self) with no parameter. This structural mismatch will cause immediate runtime errors (TypeError) or confusion when students follow the provided run example or the solution, and prevents straightforward use of the template as-is.
issues.suggested_fix: Align the template constructor with the intended usage and solution. Either (A) remove the unused initial_state parameter from the template constructor (change to def __init__(self):) so students can construct GroverLightsOutPuzzle() as shown in run() and as implemented in the solution, or (B) make initial_state optional (def __init__(self, initial_state: list[int] | None = None)) and document how/when to provide it, and update the run() example to pass an initial_state if required. Also remove any unused parameter from the template body and ensure the docstring/example matches the constructor signature.

issues.description: Constructor parameter mismatch for the Lights Out puzzle class: the template defines GroverLightsOutPuzzle.__init__(self, initial_state: list[int]) while the solution (and the problem text / run() usage) uses a no-argument constructor GroverLightsOutPuzzle.__init__(self). This creates a mapping confusion for students — the template signature suggests an initial_state must be provided when instantiating the class, but the rest of the exercise (and the reference solution) expect the initial board state to be passed later to grover_circuit via the state_of_lights argument. Students may be blocked or confused when following examples that instantiate the class without an argument or when deciding where to supply the initial state.
issues.suggested_fix: Make the template constructor signature match the solution and problem usage. Remove the unused initial_state parameter from the template constructor so it reads def __init__(self):. Alternatively, if you intend the constructor to accept the initial state, update the solution and documentation/run examples to consistently accept and use that same constructor parameter. The simplest fix: change the template constructor to def __init__(self): to align with the problem text and reference solution.
